analysis.one_liner: Gradually lowers federal sugar price supports and imports more sugar to bring sugar prices down.
analysis.headline: Despite 20 cosponsors split evenly between the parties, the bill never left the Senate Agriculture Committee and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal sugar program keeps U.S. sugar prices above world levels: the government guarantees minimum prices to sugar processors through loans, limits how much sugar those processors may sell domestically, and restricts imports through quotas. This bill would lower the guaranteed prices over time, end a program that buys up surplus sugar, phase out the sales limits, and require USDA to import enough sugar to keep supplies adequate at reasonable prices. It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: American households that buy sugar and the food manufacturers that use it in candy, cereal, baked goods, and drinks, who pay more when domestic sugar is kept scarce; and taxpayers, who are protected by a new requirement that USDA recover any program losses from sugar processors.

how_it_helps.text: Requires USDA to administer the sugar program to ensure adequate supplies of sugar at reasonable prices, and to set tariff-rate quota imports so that sugar stocks stay at targeted levels (14.5% of annual use in fiscal 2019, 15% in 2020, 15.5% thereafter).
Lowers the guaranteed loan rates for sugarcane and sugar beet processors, from 18.75 cents per pound for raw cane sugar in 2018 down to 18 cents for 2021-2023.
Ends the Feedstock Flexibility Program after 2019, under which USDA purchases surplus sugar from domestic processors and resells it to ethanol producers.
Extends, then repeals after 2020, the flexible marketing allotments that cap how much sugar domestic processing companies may sell for domestic human use.
Requires USDA to recover any net cost of the sugar program from domestic processors, shielding taxpayers from program losses.

Allows sugar-exporting countries to voluntarily transfer quota shares to one another, and expresses the sense of Congress that U.S. trade policy should pursue elimination of foreign sugar subsidies and sugar trade liberalization.

analysis.who_pays: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors — a set of producers concentrated in a handful of states — who would face lower guaranteed prices, liability for program costs, removal of sales limits, and more import competition.

drawbacks.text: The bill keeps the quota and price-support structure in place through 2023, reforming it rather than abolishing it, so consumers would still pay above-world prices for years under the bill's own terms.

Tightening supplies with more imports and lower loan rates could squeeze domestic sugar processors and growers, with job and income losses concentrated in sugar-producing regions such as the Red River Valley and south Florida.
The sense-of-Congress resolution calling for elimination of all foreign sugar subsidies is nonbinding and does not itself change trade policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the payoff is real but modest per household — sugar is a small share of food spending, though it is built into many packaged foods — while the costs fall hard on a politically concentrated group of growers and processors. Taxpayers gain from the no-net-cost guarantee. The bill is a genuine, if gradual, reform of one of the longest-standing U.S. agricultural price-support programs, not a repeal.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Agriculture Committee, which the bill was referred to on the day it was introduced, never took it up, and the 115th Congress ended with no committee or floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 7, 2017 by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen with Sen. Pat Toomey as lead cosponsor, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day.
Twenty senators cosponsored the bill: 9 Republicans and 11 Democrats.
No further action was ever taken; the committee scheduled no markup and no vote, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Domestic sugar growers and processors, who kept the price-support loans, sales limits, and import quotas untouched — leaving consumers and sugar-using food makers continuing to pay above-world prices for sugar.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no markup, no hearing action, no vote.

against.name: American Sugar Alliance
against.role: Industry group representing U.S. sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against proposals to unwind the federal sugar program, including this bill and its House companion.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines from the start: of 20 cosponsors, 11 were Democrats and 9 were Republicans, with Shaheen (D) sponsoring and Toomey (R) as lead cosponsor; opposition came from the committee process, not from a party bloc vote.

industries.industry: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors
industries.note: The current program guarantees them minimum prices through government loans, caps how much sugar they may sell domestically, buys their surplus, and restricts imports — keeping U.S. sugar prices well above world levels. The bill lowers the guarantees, makes them liable for program costs, ends surplus purchases, phases out sales limits, and lets in more imported sugar.

industries.industry: Sugar-using food manufacturers (candy, cereal, bakery, beverage)
industries.note: Their main ingredient cost falls as USDA is required to keep supplies adequate at reasonable prices and to raise quota imports toward targeted stocks levels. Groups representing these manufacturers have historically backed sugar program reform.

The Feedstock Flexibility Program, under which USDA buys surplus sugar and resells it to ethanol producers, is extended one year and then terminated, ending that discounted feedstock source after 2019.
